questions.stem: A 76 year old man of Black Caribbean heritage has 3 months of low back pain, tiredness and constipation. He is passing more urine than usual. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. He has tenderness over L2. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An older Black man with hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, normocytic anaemia and bone pain meets the CRAB pattern; a high ESR with a normal CRP points to a paraprotein.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: 76 year old man of Black Caribbean heritage
steps.x: **C**alcium high, **R**enal impairment, **A**naemia, **B**one pain: CRAB.

elim: Prostate metastases are sclerotic and do not explain renal impairment with a high ESR and normal CRP.
PMR causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness with a raised CRP.
This does not cause anaemia or a high ESR.
Sarcoid is unusual at this age and does not cause anaemia with renal failure and back pain.

steps.x: **B. Multiple myeloma.** CRAB + raised ESR with normal CRP in an older patient = myeloma.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has had three chest infections in 8 months needing antibiotics, and has lost 5 kg. She is tired and has aching ribs. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and temperature 36.9°C. Investigations: haemoglobin 101 g/L (115–165), white cell count 5.1 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 132 µmol/L (60–110), total protein 94 g/L (60–80), albumin 34 g/L (35–50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent infections, weight loss and bone pain with anaemia and a high total protein (a large globulin gap from paraprotein) suggest myeloma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Infections, weight loss and bone pain with a **high total protein but low albumin**: excess globulin.

elim: Bronchiectasis does not cause anaemia, a high total protein and bone pain.
CLL causes a lymphocytosis; her white cell count is normal.
HIV does not explain bone pain with a raised globulin and renal impairment.
Lung cancer does not cause a large globulin gap.

steps.x: **E. Multiple myeloma.** High protein, low albumin + infections + bone pain: think paraprotein.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has been monitored for 6 years with an IgG paraprotein of 9 g/L and normal blood counts. He now has back pain and fatigue. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. Investigations: haemoglobin 98 g/L (130–180), adjusted calcium 2.78 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 154 µmol/L (60–110), IgG paraprotein 34 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his new findings?
o: Progression of MGUS to multiple myeloma
questions.e: MGUS is a premalignant precursor; a rising paraprotein with new end-organ damage (CRAB) means progression to myeloma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: monitored for 6 years with an IgG paraprotein
steps.x: Known small paraprotein, now **rising** with anaemia, high calcium and renal impairment.

elim: Nothing suggests heart failure.
Waldenström's is an IgM disorder.
Osteoporosis does not raise calcium, paraprotein or creatinine.
MGUS has no end-organ damage; he now has CRAB features.

steps.x: **D. Progression of MGUS to multiple myeloma.** MGUS + new CRAB features = myeloma.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman is being investigated for an IgG paraprotein, anaemia and back pain. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and temperature 36.8°C. Her mucous membranes are dry.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Myeloma typically gives pallor, bony or vertebral tenderness, dehydration and bruising; migratory thrombophlebitis belongs to pancreatic cancer.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Anaemia (**pallor**) and bone disease (**tenderness**), plus dehydration.

elim: Clubbing is a lung or liver sign.
That suggests lymphoma or CLL.
This is Trousseau's syndrome of pancreatic cancer, not myeloma.
Virchow's node suggests gastric cancer.

steps.x: **D. Pallor with vertebral tenderness.** Myeloma on examination: pallor, bony tenderness, dehydration, bruising.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has multiple lytic lesions in his spine and pelvis. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgA band and his marrow contains 34% clonal plasma cells. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. A medical student lists features to ask about.
questions.q: Which additional feature is most likely in this condition?
o: Night sweats with rubbery lymph nodes
questions.e: Immunoparesis in myeloma causes recurrent infections. Trousseau's migratory thrombophlebitis is the classic pancreatic cancer distractor.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Confirmed **myeloma**: normal antibodies are suppressed.

elim: Not a feature of myeloma.
This is a pancreatic cancer feature, not classic myeloma.
These suggest lymphoma.
This suggests pancreatic head cancer.

steps.x: **E. Recurrent bacterial infections.** Myeloma: infections, yes; migratory thrombophlebitis, no.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman fractured her right humerus reaching for a shelf. She has no history of cancer. X-ray shows a fracture through a well-defined lytic lesion with no sclerotic rim. Investigations: haemoglobin 99 g/L (115–165), adjusted calcium 2.81 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 146 µmol/L (60–110), ALP 92 U/L (30–130).
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her fracture?
questions.e: A pathological fracture through a lytic lesion with anaemia, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment is myeloma; ALP is normal because osteoblasts are suppressed.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: lytic lesion with no sclerotic rim
steps.x: Low-trauma fracture through a **lytic** lesion, CRAB bloods, **normal ALP**.

elim: Osteoporosis has a normal bone profile and no lytic lesion.
Paget's has a very high ALP and mixed sclerotic changes.
This does not cause anaemia and renal impairment with a lytic lesion.
Bone cysts occur in children and do not cause CRAB features.

steps.x: **A. Multiple myeloma.** Lytic lesions with normal ALP = myeloma.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with multiple myeloma is brought in with 3 days of increasing drowsiness, vomiting and thirst. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. He has no focal neurology. Investigations: sodium 139 mmol/L (135–145), glucose 6.0 mmol/L, adjusted calcium 3.46 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 198 µmol/L (60–110).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his drowsiness?
questions.e: Bone resorption in myeloma causes hypercalcaemia; over 3.4 with confusion, vomiting and dehydration is a hypercalcaemic crisis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Confusion, vomiting, dehydration and **calcium 3.46**.

elim: There is no focal neurology and myeloma rarely spreads to brain.
His glucose is normal.
His sodium is normal.
He is afebrile, and the calcium explains the picture.

steps.x: **B. Hypercalcaemic crisis.** Confused myeloma patient: check calcium.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man is referred with an AKI found on routine bloods. He has had back pain for 4 months. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. Urine dipstick is negative for blood and protein, but urine protein:creatinine ratio is markedly raised. Investigations: haemoglobin 89 g/L (130–180), adjusted calcium 2.92 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 412 µmol/L (60–110).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Dipstick detects albumin, not light chains, so a negative dipstick with a high PCR suggests Bence Jones proteinuria; with anaemia, hypercalcaemia and back pain this is myeloma kidney.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
AKI with **dipstick-negative proteinuria**: the protein is not albumin.

elim: Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.
This would not cause heavy proteinuria, anaemia and back pain.
RPGN gives blood and protein on dipstick.
Rhabdomyolysis gives blood on dipstick and does not cause hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: **A. Multiple myeloma.** Negative dipstick but high PCR = light chains.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with newly diagnosed myeloma is pale and tired. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. Her ferritin, B12 and folate are normal. A full blood count is sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?
questions.e: Marrow infiltration by plasma cells crowds out red cell production, giving a normocytic normochromic anaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: ferritin, B12 and folate are normal
steps.x: Haematinics normal: anaemia from **marrow infiltration**.

elim: That is CLL.
That is B12 or folate deficiency; both are normal.
That suggests iron deficiency; ferritin is normal.
Myeloma causes anaemia, not polycythaemia.

steps.x: **D. Normocytic normochromic anaemia.** Myeloma anaemia is normocytic and normochromic.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has 2 months of constant thoracic back pain that wakes him at night, with fatigue. He has no morning stiffness of his shoulders or hips. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Night pain with anaemia and hypercalcaemia is a red flag; a very high ESR with a normal CRP suggests a paraprotein, as in myeloma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Red-flag back pain with **high ESR but normal CRP**.

elim: AS starts in young adults with morning stiffness and raised CRP.
Mechanical pain does not wake him nightly with anaemia and high calcium.
Osteoporosis has normal ESR and calcium.
PMR has girdle stiffness and a raised CRP.

steps.x: **C. Multiple myeloma.** High ESR, normal CRP: think paraprotein.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with bone pain and anaemia has a skeletal X-ray series. The lateral skull film shows multiple small, round, well-defined lucencies of similar size scattered across the vault, with no sclerotic margins. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Multiple punched-out lytic lesions on the skull give the classic 'raindrop skull' of myeloma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Punched-out lucencies like **raindrops** on the vault.

elim: This gives a 'pepper-pot' skull of fine granular mottling.
Osteoporosis does not cause punched-out lesions.
Paget's gives a thickened 'cotton-wool' skull.
These are dense sclerotic lesions, and she is a woman.

steps.x: **B. Multiple myeloma.** Raindrop skull = myeloma; pepper-pot = hyperparathyroidism; cotton-wool = Paget's.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has fatigue and aching bones. She has no headache, jaw pain or shoulder stiffness. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 126/76 mmHg. Her ESR is 118 mm/h (<20) and CRP 4 mg/L (<5). Her blood film shows red cells stacked together like piles of coins.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rouleaux (stacked red cells) form when paraprotein coats red cells, raising the ESR without raising CRP: a diagnostic clue to myeloma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
**Rouleaux** with a very high ESR and normal CRP.

elim: No headache or jaw claudication, and CRP would be raised.
Lymphoma does not typically cause rouleaux with a normal CRP.
No shoulder stiffness, and CRP would be raised.
TB raises CRP and does not cause marked rouleaux.

steps.x: **C. Multiple myeloma.** Rouleaux on the film = paraprotein = myeloma clue.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with myeloma has 4 days of severe mid-back pain and now his legs feel heavy and numb. He has not opened his bowels for 3 days. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
o: Bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level
Isolated foot drop on one side
questions.e: Vertebral collapse or plasmacytoma can compress the cord, giving bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level and sphincter disturbance.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Back pain + bilateral leg symptoms + bowel change: **cord compression**.

elim: That is a radial nerve problem.
That is a peripheral neuropathy.
That suggests a common peroneal nerve palsy.
That is a facial nerve or stroke sign.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level.** Myeloma + back pain + leg signs = cord compression until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman has fatigue and constipation. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.84 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 0.9 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), haemoglobin 102 g/L (115–165), creatinine 138 µmol/L (60–110), total protein 92 g/L (60–80).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia with a suppressed PTH, anaemia, renal impairment and high total protein suggests myeloma; SPEP is the best initial test.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
PTH-independent hypercalcaemia with a **globulin gap**.

elim: Bone scans miss myeloma lesions.
Sarcoid is less likely with anaemia, renal impairment and high total protein.
Myeloma is more likely given the high total protein.
PTH is suppressed, so this is not hyperparathyroidism.

steps.x: **C. Serum protein electrophoresis.** Suspected myeloma: start with serum protein electrophoresis.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has lytic lesions, anaemia and an AKI. Serum protein electrophoresis shows no monoclonal band and his immunoglobulins are low. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. The haematologist still suspects myeloma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next blood test?
questions.e: Light-chain myeloma makes only free light chains, which may not show on SPEP; the full myeloma screen includes serum free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
CRAB features but **SPEP negative**: think light-chain only.

elim: ANA does not detect plasma cell disorders.
ACE is for sarcoidosis.
Ferritin does not detect a paraprotein.
PSA screens for prostate cancer, which gives sclerotic lesions.

steps.x: **D. Serum free light chains.** Myeloma screen = SPEP + serum free light chains + urine Bence Jones.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has back pain, anaemia and a creatinine of 186 µmol/L (60–110). Urine dipstick is negative for protein. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. The team wants a urine test to complete the myeloma screen.
questions.q: Which urine test is most appropriate?
o: Urine electrophoresis for Bence Jones protein
questions.e: Bence Jones proteins are free light chains, missed by dipstick; urine electrophoresis detects them.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Dipstick misses light chains; you need a test that **separates proteins**.

elim: Dipstick detects albumin, not light chains.
ACR measures albumin, not light chains.
Nothing suggests infection.
Microscopy does not identify the protein.

steps.x: **D. Urine electrophoresis for Bence Jones protein.** Urine Bence Jones protein is part of every myeloma screen.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has an IgG paraprotein of 38 g/L, a haemoglobin of 96 g/L (130–180) and lytic lesions on whole-body low-dose CT. He undergoes a bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which marrow finding confirms the diagnosis?
o: Small mature lymphocytes replacing the marrow
questions.e: The gold standard is a myeloma screen plus marrow biopsy; more than 10% clonal plasma cells confirms myeloma.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.

clues: bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
steps.x: Paraprotein and end-organ damage: the marrow must show a **plasma cell clone**.

elim: Myeloblasts suggest acute myeloid leukaemia.
That suggests myelofibrosis.
Ring sideroblasts suggest myelodysplasia.
That suggests CLL.

steps.x: **C. More than 10% clonal plasma cells.** Marrow >10% clonal plasma cells confirms myeloma.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has newly diagnosed myeloma on marrow biopsy. She has rib and back pain. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. An isotope bone scan arranged by her GP last month was reported as normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging to assess her bone disease?
o: Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine only
questions.e: Whole-body low-dose CT is first-line imaging for myeloma bone disease; isotope scans are often falsely normal because osteoblasts are suppressed.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Bone scan normal despite pain: myeloma lesions are **purely lytic**.

elim: DEXA measures density, not lytic lesions.
Brain imaging does not assess skeletal disease.
A single X-ray misses most lesions.
Bone scans miss lytic myeloma lesions.

steps.x: **E. Whole-body low-dose CT.** Myeloma imaging: whole-body low-dose CT.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man is suspected of having multiple myeloma because of back pain and a monoclonal band. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. His GP asks what routine bloods would typically show.
questions.q: Which set of results is most likely?
o: High Hb, low calcium, normal ESR, high CRP
Low Hb, high calcium, high ESR, normal CRP
Low Hb, low calcium, high ESR, high CRP
Low Hb, normal calcium, normal ESR, high CRP
Normal Hb, high calcium, normal ESR, normal CRP
questions.e: Myeloma typically gives a normocytic anaemia, raised calcium, renal impairment and a raised ESR with normal CRP.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.

clues: back pain and a monoclonal band
steps.x: Paraprotein raises the ESR, not the CRP.

elim: Myeloma causes anaemia and hypercalcaemia.
Calcium is high in myeloma, and CRP is usually normal.
This suits infection or inflammation.
This suits hyperparathyroidism.

steps.x: **B. Low Hb, high calcium, high ESR, normal CRP.** Myeloma bloods: low Hb, high calcium, high creatinine, high ESR, normal CRP.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with myeloma has 2 days of worsening thoracic back pain and difficulty walking. She has brisk knee reflexes and reduced sensation below the umbilicus. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. She has been given dexamethasone.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours
Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine
questions.e: Suspected malignant spinal cord compression needs an emergency whole-spine MRI, as myeloma often affects several levels.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.

clues: thoracic back pain and difficulty walking
steps.x: Upper motor neurone leg signs and a **sensory level**.

elim: The signs localise to the thoracic cord.
Bone scans miss myeloma and do not show the cord.
LP is contraindicated and unhelpful in suspected compression.
X-rays cannot show cord compression.

steps.x: **D. MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours.** Suspected cord compression: emergency whole-spine MRI.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman with frailty, heart failure and newly diagnosed symptomatic myeloma is not eligible for stem cell transplantation. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 126/72 mmHg. The haematology MDT discusses an established first-line regimen for older patients.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Older, transplant-ineligible patients can be treated with MPT (melphalan, prednisolone, thalidomide) or other systemic anti-myeloma therapy.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: not eligible for stem cell transplantation
steps.x: Older and **transplant-ineligible**.

elim: She is not eligible for transplant.
Imatinib is for chronic myeloid leukaemia.
R-CHOP is for diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
Symptomatic myeloma needs treatment.

steps.x: **C. Melphalan, prednisolone and thalidomide.** Older patients: MPT; fit patients: induction then autologous transplant.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has newly diagnosed multiple myeloma with lytic lesions and anaemia. He is fit, runs twice a week and has no other conditions. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. He will be considered for transplant later.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: First-line treatment is systemic anti-myeloma therapy such as a bortezomib/dexamethasone-based regimen, then autologous transplant if fit.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Fit patient: needs **induction** first, transplant later.

elim: ABVD is for Hodgkin lymphoma.
Hydroxycarbamide is for myeloproliferative disorders.
Local radiotherapy does not treat systemic disease.
Rituximab targets CD20, not plasma cells.

steps.x: **B. Bortezomib and dexamethasone-based induction.** First line: bortezomib/dexamethasone-based therapy.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman with myeloma has completed four cycles of bortezomib-based induction and is in very good partial response. She works full time and has no comorbidities. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Allogeneic transplant from an unrelated donor
questions.e: In younger, fitter patients the gold-standard consolidation after induction is high-dose melphalan with autologous stem cell transplantation.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Young, fit, **responded** to induction.

elim: Allogeneic transplant is not standard first-line for myeloma.
MPT is for older transplant-ineligible patients.
Splenectomy has no role.
Fit patients benefit from consolidation with transplant.

steps.x: **B. Autologous stem cell transplantation.** Fit patients: induction then autologous stem cell transplant.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man starts treatment for myeloma with lytic lesions in his ribs and pelvis. His dentist has checked his teeth. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. His calcium is 2.48 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and creatinine 98 µmol/L (60–110). The team wants to reduce future fractures.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Bisphosphonates (e.g. zoledronic acid) reduce skeletal events in myeloma; a dental check first reduces the risk of jaw osteonecrosis.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: lytic lesions in his ribs and pelvis
steps.x: Bone disease, dental check done: **bone protection**.

elim: Not used for myeloma bone disease.
This does not reduce myeloma bone events enough.
Not indicated in a man with myeloma bone disease.
Teriparatide is avoided in malignancy involving bone.

steps.x: **A. Bisphosphonate.** Myeloma bone protection: bisphosphonates.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with myeloma has rib pain not controlled by regular paracetamol. Her creatinine is 156 µmol/L (60–110). Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. She asks for something stronger.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to her analgesia?
o: Oral morphine at a reduced dose
questions.e: NSAIDs should be avoided in myeloma because they can precipitate renal failure; step up to an opioid, adjusting for renal function.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Myeloma with **impaired kidneys**: no NSAIDs.

elim: Anti-inflammatory doses of aspirin are nephrotoxic like other NSAIDs.
NSAIDs can precipitate renal failure in myeloma.
NSAIDs can precipitate renal failure in myeloma.
Uncontrolled pain needs stepping up the analgesic ladder.

steps.x: **E. Oral morphine at a reduced dose.** Avoid NSAIDs in myeloma.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with myeloma is confused and has vomited for 2 days. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and his mucous membranes are dry. Investigations: adjusted calcium 3.52 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 188 µmol/L (60–110), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5–5.3).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemic crisis needs urgent correction: aggressive IV 0.9% saline first, then an IV bisphosphonate.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Severe hypercalcaemia with **dehydration**.

elim: Calcium would worsen hypercalcaemia.
Loop diuretics worsen dehydration and are not first-line.
Oral bisphosphonates act too slowly.
Thiazides raise calcium.

steps.x: **A. IV 0.9% sodium chloride.** Hypercalcaemic crisis: IV saline first.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with newly diagnosed myeloma has a creatinine that has risen from 140 to 320 µmol/L (60–110) over a week. Urine shows heavy Bence Jones proteinuria. She is not overloaded. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg. Calcium is 2.62 mmol/L (2.20–2.60).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV contrast CT to assess the kidneys
IV fluids and stop nephrotoxic drugs
questions.e: Myeloma kidney is worsened by dehydration, hypercalcaemia and nephrotoxins; give fluids, stop nephrotoxics and start urgent anti-myeloma treatment.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Light chain AKI: **dilute** the light chains, remove nephrotoxins.

elim: Dehydration worsens cast nephropathy.
Contrast is nephrotoxic.
Treatment should not wait for biopsy.
NSAIDs worsen renal injury.

steps.x: **C. IV fluids and stop nephrotoxic drugs.** Myeloma AKI: fluids, stop nephrotoxics, treat the myeloma urgently.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with myeloma on bortezomib and dexamethasone has a 1 day history of fever, rigors and a cough. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Give the next cycle of bortezomib
Oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours
questions.e: Myeloma and its treatment cause immunosuppression; sepsis needs urgent IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, within an hour.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Immunosuppressed and **septic**.

elim: Chemotherapy is held during sepsis.
Steroids do not treat infection.
He is septic and immunosuppressed; oral therapy is inadequate.
Delay increases mortality in sepsis.

steps.x: **C. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.** Sepsis in myeloma: IV antibiotics within the hour.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with myeloma has severe thoracic back pain and has developed leg weakness over 24 hours. He has a sensory level at T10. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. An emergency MRI has been requested.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate drug treatment?
questions.e: Suspected malignant cord compression is treated with high-dose dexamethasone while emergency MRI and definitive treatment (radiotherapy or surgery) are arranged.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Malignant **cord compression**: reduce oedema now.

elim: Bisphosphonates do not relieve cord compression.
Anticoagulation does not treat compression.
NSAIDs are avoided in myeloma and do not treat compression.
This dose is far too low.

steps.x: **A. Dexamethasone 16 mg.** Cord compression: dexamethasone 16 mg + emergency MRI.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has myeloma confirmed on marrow biopsy. The haematologist explains that the malignant cells are terminally differentiated, make one type of immunoglobulin and have passed through the germinal centre.
questions.q: Which cell is the origin of her malignancy?
questions.e: Myeloma is a clonal malignancy of plasma cells, post-germinal centre B cells that secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin (paraprotein).

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Antibody-secreting, **post-germinal centre** B cell.

elim: Mast cell disease is mastocytosis.
These make platelets.
Myeloblasts give acute myeloid leukaemia.
Naive B cells have not passed through the germinal centre.

steps.x: **E. Plasma cell.** Myeloma = clonal plasma cells making one paraprotein.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with myeloma has multiple lytic lesions in his pelvis and femurs. His ALP is normal. A researcher explains how myeloma cells interact with bone cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lytic lesions?
o: Increased osteoblast activity with woven bone
RANKL and IL-6 activate osteoclasts while osteoblasts are suppressed
questions.e: Myeloma cells release RANKL and IL-6, activating osteoclasts, while suppressing osteoblasts: net resorption gives lytic lesions and a normal ALP.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Lytic lesions with **no** osteoblast response (normal ALP).

elim: That is osteomalacia.
PTH is suppressed in myeloma.
That is Paget's or sclerotic metastases.
That is postmenopausal osteoporosis.

steps.x: **D. RANKL and IL-6 activate osteoclasts while osteoblasts are suppressed.** Myeloma bone: osteoclasts up (RANKL, IL-6), osteoblasts down.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has extensive lytic lesions on whole-body low-dose CT due to myeloma. An isotope bone scan done earlier showed no increased uptake. Her ALP is 84 U/L (30–130).
questions.q: Which best explains the normal bone scan?
o: Lesions are too small to detect

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with myeloma has an adjusted calcium of 3.04 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and a PTH of 0.8 pmol/L (1.6–8.5). His PTH-related peptide is not raised and his vitamin D is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypercalcaemia?
o: Reduced renal calcium excretion from thiazides
questions.e: In myeloma, cytokine-driven osteoclast activity resorbs bone and releases calcium into the blood; PTH is appropriately suppressed.

questions.e: Filtered light chains bind uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) in the distal tubule to form obstructing casts (myeloma cast nephropathy), worsened by dehydration and hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with myeloma has a fever, productive cough and right lower zone consolidation. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. Her IgG paraprotein is high but her IgA and IgM are very low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Immunoparesis (low normal immunoglobulins) leaves myeloma patients vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae.

steps.x: Functional **antibody deficiency**: encapsulated bacteria.
